questions.q: What is the normal oral body temperature?
questions.explain: Normal range is about 36.5–37.5 °C.

open.q: What is the normal oral body temperature?

questions.q: How does rectal temperature compare with oral temperature?
questions.explain: Rectal temperature is closest to core temperature.

open.q: How does rectal temperature compare with oral temperature?

questions.q: How does axillary temperature compare with oral temperature?
questions.explain: The skin is cooler than the core.

open.q: How does axillary temperature compare with oral temperature?

questions.q: At what time of day is body temperature lowest?
questions.explain: Temperature has a circadian rhythm with a peak in the late afternoon or evening, a range of about 1 °C.

open.q: At what time of day is body temperature lowest?

questions.q: What is the main route of heat loss in a comfortable room at rest?
questions.explain: Radiation accounts for about 60% of heat loss under these conditions.

open.q: What is the main route of heat loss in a comfortable room at rest?

questions.q: When ambient temperature exceeds skin temperature, which mechanism remains effective for net heat loss?
questions.explain: When the environment is hotter than the skin, radiation, conduction and convection may transfer heat into the body; evaporation is the effective route for net heat loss.

open.q: When the surrounding temperature is higher than body temperature, heat is lost only by:

questions.q: Where is the thermoregulatory centre?
questions.explain: The preoptic area of the hypothalamus contains temperature-sensitive neurons.

open.q: Where is the thermoregulatory centre?

questions.q: Which part of the hypothalamus is the heat-loss centre?
questions.explain: Stimulation causes vasodilation and sweating.

open.q: Which part of the hypothalamus is the heat-loss centre?

questions.q: Which part of the hypothalamus is the heat-gain (heat-promoting) centre?
questions.explain: Stimulation causes vasoconstriction, shivering and increased metabolism.

open.q: Which part of the hypothalamus is the heat-gain (heat-promoting) centre?

questions.q: Name two responses to cold exposure.
questions.explain: Other responses include piloerection, increased thyroxine and adrenaline, and brown fat thermogenesis in infants.

open.q: Name two responses to cold exposure.
open.a: Shivering and cutaneous vasoconstriction (also piloerection, more thyroxine and adrenaline)

questions.q: Name two responses to heat exposure.
questions.explain: Reduced appetite and muscle activity also lower heat production.

open.q: Name two responses to heat exposure.
open.a: Sweating and cutaneous vasodilation (also reduced appetite and activity)

questions.q: How do pyrogens cause fever?
options: IL-1 and PGE2 raise the hypothalamic set point
questions.explain: The body then behaves as if too cold, causing vasoconstriction and shivering until the new set point is reached.

open.q: How do pyrogens cause fever?

questions.q: How do antipyretics such as aspirin and paracetamol lower fever?
options: By inhibiting interleukin-1 release from bacteria
questions.explain: Lower PGE2 in the hypothalamus returns the set point to normal.

open.q: How do antipyretics such as aspirin and paracetamol lower fever?

questions.q: What distinguishes heat stroke from heat exhaustion?
options: Core temperature above about 40 °C with central nervous system dysfunction
Profuse sweating with a normal core temperature
A raised hypothalamic set point caused by PGE2
Shivering with a falling core temperature
questions.explain: Heat stroke is defined by severe hyperthermia with central nervous system dysfunction. Sweating may be present, particularly in exertional heat stroke, so anhidrosis is not a required distinguishing feature.

open.q: What distinguishes heat stroke from heat exhaustion?

questions.q: Which hormone increases heat production over days to weeks of cold exposure?
questions.explain: It raises basal metabolic rate.

open.q: Which hormone increases heat production over days to weeks of cold exposure?

questions.q: How does brown fat generate heat?
questions.explain: Energy from the proton gradient is released as heat instead of making ATP. It is important in newborns.

open.q: How does brown fat generate heat?

questions.q: During exposure to a cold environment, which hypothalamic response helps conserve body heat?
questions.explain: Cold-sensitive pathways activate hypothalamic heat-conservation responses, including cutaneous vasoconstriction, which reduces heat transfer from the body core to the skin.

open.q: What cutaneous vascular response helps conserve heat during cold exposure?

questions.q: A patient with severe heat stroke has a core temperature of 41.5 °C and altered mental status after prolonged exertion. Which feature best distinguishes this condition from an uncomplicated fever?
options: The hypothalamic set point is raised by prostaglandin E2
Heat production is always increased by shivering
Thermoregulatory heat loss is overwhelmed without a raised hypothalamic set point
The hypothalamus deliberately maintains a higher set point
questions.explain: Heat stroke is a form of hyperthermia in which heat gain or production exceeds heat dissipation; the hypothalamic set point is not reset upward as it is in fever.

open.q: What distinguishes heat stroke from fever at the hypothalamic level?

questions.q: A newborn has limited ability to shiver but can generate heat through brown adipose tissue. Which mechanism is responsible?
options: Uncoupling of oxidative phosphorylation by thermogenin (UCP1)
Inhibition of the electron transport chain by cyanide
Increased ATP synthesis through ATP synthase
questions.explain: Thermogenin (uncoupling protein 1) in brown-fat mitochondria permits proton re-entry without ATP synthesis, dissipating the proton gradient as heat.

open.q: Which mitochondrial protein mediates non-shivering thermogenesis in brown adipose tissue?

questions.q: During prolonged exposure to a hot environment, a previously unacclimatised worker begins to sweat more efficiently. Which adaptation is expected with heat acclimatisation?
options: Reduced sweat production and increased sodium loss
Earlier onset of sweating with more dilute sweat
A higher core-temperature threshold for sweating
questions.explain: Heat acclimatisation increases sweating capacity and promotes earlier sweating; aldosterone-mediated sodium conservation makes sweat more dilute, reducing salt loss.

open.q: What happens to sweating during heat acclimatisation?
accept: increased sweating with reduced salt loss

questions.q: A person immersed in cold water loses body heat rapidly. Which physical principle explains why this environment can cause faster heat loss than exposure to cold air at the same temperature?
options: Water has a much greater capacity to transfer heat from the body than air
Water prevents conduction from the skin
The body loses heat only by evaporation in water
Water increases the hypothalamic set point
questions.explain: Water conducts and convects heat away from the body much more effectively than air, so immersion can produce rapid core cooling even at comparable ambient temperatures.

open.q: Why does immersion in cold water cause rapid heat loss compared with cold air?

questions.q: A febrile patient is given an antipyretic drug that inhibits cyclo-oxygenase. What is the immediate thermoregulatory consequence?
options: The hypothalamic set point rises further
Prostaglandin E2 synthesis falls and the set point returns toward normal
Brown adipose tissue thermogenesis becomes obligatory
questions.explain: Cyclo-oxygenase inhibition reduces hypothalamic prostaglandin E2 production, reversing the fever-associated elevation in the thermoregulatory set point and allowing heat-loss responses.

open.q: How do cyclo-oxygenase-inhibiting antipyretics reduce fever?

questions.q: A worker newly transferred to a hot, humid environment gradually becomes better able to tolerate prolonged work in the heat. Which change is characteristic of heat acclimatisation?
options: Earlier onset of sweating with a more dilute sweat
Reduced plasma volume and increased salt loss
questions.explain: Heat acclimatisation produces earlier, more profuse and more dilute sweating, alongside plasma-volume expansion and improved cardiovascular stability.

questions.q: A person exposed to cold begins to shiver. Which mechanism accounts for the increased heat production?
questions.explain: Shivering consists of involuntary skeletal-muscle contractions that increase metabolic heat production without producing useful external work.

questions.q: A patient with a hypothalamic lesion cannot mount an appropriate response to a fall in core temperature. Which normal response would have helped conserve heat?
options: Increased blood flow to the skin
questions.explain: Cold defence includes cutaneous vasoconstriction to reduce heat transfer from the core to the skin and inhibition of sweating.

questions.q: A patient is cooled in a room where the surrounding surfaces are substantially colder than the skin. Which mode of heat transfer can occur without direct physical contact?
questions.explain: Radiation transfers heat by electromagnetic waves between surfaces at different temperatures and does not require direct contact.

questions.q: During the rising phase of an infection-related fever, a patient feels cold and develops chills even though the measured core temperature is elevated. What best explains this sensation?
options: The hypothalamic set point has risen, making the current temperature feel too low
The hypothalamic set point has fallen below normal
Sweating has increased the core temperature
Pyrogens have permanently damaged peripheral thermoreceptors
questions.explain: Pyrogen-mediated prostaglandin E2 raises the hypothalamic set point. Until core temperature reaches the new set point, vasoconstriction and shivering are triggered and the patient feels cold.
